description:
A multidisciplinary team combining robotics, AI, computer science, mechanical engineering, and full-stack development. Work spans multi-UAV vision, industrial AI, secure IoT, and motion capture. We use Python, C/C++, PyTorch, OpenCV, Docker, Linux, STM32, ESP32, FPGA, DSP, CAD, and Unity. From algorithms to complete applications, we turn complex ideas into working systems.
The burn wasn't scheduled. The execution will be.
Think big. Engineer carefully. Build fast. Test everything.
summary:
Lunar Site Navigator is a browser-based tool for planning a landing and a rover drive at the lunar south pole. It runs offline and uses real NASA data. Near the pole the Sun barely rises above the horizon and crater rims cast long shadows. That makes a landing site as much a date as a place: the same spot can have sunlight and an Earth link one week and lose both the next.

The tool combines LRO LOLA elevation maps (down to 5 m), permanently shadowed regions, Diviner data on where ice could survive, and JPL Horizons positions for the Sun and Earth. For any site and date, it checks whether the Sun and Earth clear the real terrain skyline. It also shows how the outlook changes if the landing slips, and finds better spots nearby. It suggests rover routes and checks each one for slopes, battery energy, radio coverage and the nearest safe place to wait.

The user picks the site and route on a 3D Moon, freezes the plan, then watches a simulated lander fly it from launch to touchdown and drive the route. Early missions can then screen landing dates in minutes, using open data and clearly labelled assumptions.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Site Navigator plans a landing and a rover drive at the lunar south pole. Near the pole the Sun stays low and crater rims cast long shadows, so a site that is sunlit and in contact with Earth one week can be dark and out of contact the next. The tool turns that into a clear, checkable plan in three steps:

  1. Map (Plan). Pick a site anywhere on a 3D Moon, from the whole globe down to 20 m detail at the pole. For a landing date, the tool takes the real terrain skyline around the spot and checks when the Sun and Earth rise above it. It reports:
    “Where to land” scores a whole landing ellipse. Other layers show permanently shadowed regions, NASA’s 18.6-year average illumination, slope, possible ice (thermal stability, not detection) and solar energy for the lander’s panels.
    • how many hours of the stay have both in view
    • how that changes if the landing slips
    • which nearby spots do better
  2. Rover route. Draw or type a route. The tool offers three candidates, shortest, flattest and sunniest, found with an A* search under direction-dependent slope limits, plus a B-RRT* self-driving planner. The chosen route is checked for:
    • Mobility: climb, descent and cross-slope limits, one-way stretches and ground the rover can’t drive back out of
    • Energy: a timed simulation where the panels only work while the Sun clears the local skyline, with battery level, recharge stops and departure times that work
    • Communications: coverage from a surface station over the terrain, using free-space loss and knife-edge diffraction
    • Contingency: the nearest safe place to wait from every 2 km of the route
  3. Finalise and Execute (Fly). Finalise runs a go / no-go check and freezes the plan. Execute then flies exactly that plan with a generic robotic lander:
    • launch, transfer, lunar orbit insertion and powered descent
    • Δv and propellant budget, with lunar gravity effects (J2/C22) and the pull of Earth and Sun
    • contingency branches: abort, divert, wave-off and hold
    • the planned rover drive on the 3D globe

An MCP server exposes the same calculations to AI assistants, so a planner can ask questions like “best landing dates at Shackleton in 2027” in plain language.

Benefits

  • Screening a landing date takes minutes, not a specialist study.
  • Site, date, route and vehicle are checked together, in one place.
  • Everything runs offline in a browser, with no install, account or licence.
  • Every vehicle, battery, panel and radio figure is labelled as an assumption the user can change.
  • Missions save as JSON, GeoJSON or CSV.

Intended impact

Artemis, CLPS and international missions are all heading for the south pole. Small teams, universities and students need a quick, open first-look tool before they commit to detailed analysis. The aim is to make “is this site good on this date, and can the rover get back?” a question anyone can answer from public NASA data. It is meant for screening, not certified landing analysis, and the tool says so.

Tools, languages, software and hardware

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules) in the browser; Node 22 build and data scripts with no npm dependencies; HTML/CSS
  • Libraries: three.js (3D globe), driver.js (guided tour), deep-chat (assistant panel)
  • Testing: the Node test runner, with 188 test files
  • AI integration: an MCP server for AI assistants
  • NASA and science data:
    • LRO LOLA elevation maps (global, plus polar maps down to 5 m) and SLDEM2015
    • Mazarico et al. shadowed-region and illumination maps
    • Diviner ice-stability grids
    • JPL Horizons ephemeris
    • GRAIL gravity model GRGM900C
    • the JPL lunar surface station paper
    • ITU-R P.526 (diffraction)
    • USGS planetary names
  • AI tools (declared in the repo): Claude Code wrote most of the code; an OpenAI model through opencode implemented some modules
  • Hardware: none beyond ordinary laptops

Creativity

The tool treats a landing site as a place and a time window, and shows how the answer changes if the landing slips. It also links planning to flying: the plan frozen in Finalise is exactly what the lander flies and the rover drives. The overview page has small interactive models of the skyline test, the site search and the route search, so a non-specialist can see how each algorithm works.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and honesty: real terrain and ephemeris; limits and resolution shown on every result; assumptions labelled
  • Accessibility and cost: free, open source (MIT), runs offline, no sign-up, works on a modest laptop
  • Energy: solar power and battery are modelled explicitly, because they decide whether a polar mission survives
  • Safety: contingency rules for both the lander and the rover
  • Compliance: every dataset and AI use is credited; no NASA logos or mission identifiers
